title: Diurnal hysteresis throughput & latency log
content:
Context:
This is a personal scratchpad summarizing a set of experiments run to understand why tail latency and p99s spike during the *falling edge* of a sustained high-load window (the diurnal decline) even after request QPS is reduced. We've seen similar symptoms in customer reports (esp. multi-tenant Dedicated pools) where traffic drops but latency doesn't immediately recover.

Hypothesis:
1) Hysteresis: resource/queueing/kv-cache state persists after sustained high load; when QPS drops, small batches + cache misses cause serialization and elevated p99s.
2) Warm/cold path mix: during high load GPUs run with large KV cache residency and long prefix reuse; when load drops, many requests are for new prefixes causing cache churn and backend stalls.
3) Autoscaler/eviction artifacts: quick scale-downs or eviction of warm workers cause a short period where requests are distributed to fewer but cold workers.

Experiment matrix (runs run across 3 node pools, 2 model sizes):
- Model variants: small-7B (fp16, quant q4_0), medium-13B (int8-like sim).
- Node hardware: gpus-a100-80g, gpus-h100-80g (simulated in cluster).
- KV cache configs: default (LRU, 30m expiry), sticky (longer TTL 4h), aggressive-evict (10m).
- Arrival pattern: synthetic diurnal (24h compressed to 6h for test) with: 2h ramp-up, 2h sustained-high, 1h ramp-down, 1h low. Peak QPS chosen to saturate pool (~85% util).
- Autoscaler profiles: conservative (scale down delay 10m), aggressive (2m), no-scale (pinned).

Key runs (timestamps are local test times):
1) 2025-11-11 09:00 - baseline steady QPS 100 for 1h (warm cache).
   - small-7B on a100: p50=32ms, p95=120ms, p99=280ms, throughput=980 req/s, kv-hit=78%
2) 2025-11-11 10:30 - diurnal compress: ramp-up -> sustain 5m -> ramp-down to low over 2m (shortened for stress).
   - Observed immediate p99 spike on ramp-down: p99 jumped from 280ms -> 850ms for ~40s window. p95 had smaller bump (120->220ms). kv-hit dropped 78% -> 41% during spike.
3) 2025-11-12 03:00 - autoscaler aggressive + kv-cache sticky
   - p99 bump reduced: 280ms -> 470ms for 20s. kv-hit maintained at ~65%.
4) 2025-11-12 08:15 - autoscaler conservative + aggressive-evict
   - Worse tail: p99 peaked 1.2s and sustained for ~90s after drop. Observed several worker restarts/evictions in logs (pod churn).

Micro-observations / traces:
- Trace snippets show long waits in request queue layer while batch builder attempts to form minimum batch size. When QPS drops, batch sizes shrink and processing becomes less efficient (kernel startup overheads dominate).
- GPU metrics show warm kernel occupancy but then a flurry of small kernels after ramp-down (high kernel setup %).
- KV cache eviction logs correlate tightly with p99 windows. When eviction TTL short, many new prefix loads hit disk/host memory and introduce serialization in the runtime.
- In some runs there are short-lived GC-like pauses in runtime when many small tensors are deallocated simultaneously (suspect: hotpath memory allocator behavior under changing batch sizes).

Quantitative summary (selected):
- Best case (sticky-kv, conservative-scale): p99 recovery time ~18s, p99 delta ~+220ms over baseline. kv-hit ~70%.
- Worst case (aggressive-evict, aggressive-scale): p99 recovery time ~95s, p99 delta ~+900ms. kv-hit falls below 35%.
- Throughput drop is immediate as QPS reduces (by definition), but effective service time increases which reduces headroom for remaining requests and amplifies tail.

Interpretation / short circuit:
1) KV cache warmness is a dominant factor. Sustained-high periods build a working set in cache; once load declines the mix of requests shifts to lower reuse and triggers cache churn. Short TTLs or eviction policies make this worse.
2) Autoscaler timing interacts badly: aggressive scale-downs remove warm capacity, forcing remaining workers to handle cold-loads, increasing p99. Conservative scaling keeps warm workers and reduces tail.
3) Batching logic needs to be adaptive: current min-batch thresholds and timeouts assume steady arrival; under quick falling edges they create tiny batches that are expensive per-request. Dynamic preference for slightly larger batches during falling edges could amortize overhead.
4) Memory allocator and kernel-launch overheads are non-trivial contributors when batch sizes shrink suddenly.

Immediate mitigations (to prototype):
- Increase kv-cache TTL for Dedicated pools with diurnal traffic (config flag: kv_ttl_hint).
- Add a scale-down cooldown that respects recent sustained-high windows (scale_down_delay = max(2m, 0.5 * sustained_window)).
- Introduce a "falling-edge" detector: when slope of QPS(t) < -threshold, temporarily bump batch-timeout to avoid hammering with tiny batches for next X seconds.
- Add lightweight background pre-warm threads that keep one or two workers lightly active during early scale-down to maintain KV warmed pages.

Next experiments (planned):
- Run with realistic customer traces (anonymized) to validate whether synthetic diurnal is representative.
- Test explicit "prefetch prefixes" strategy: on sustained-high, compute top-K prefixes and feed them to cache preloader during ramp-down. Measure kv-hit and p99 impact.
- Allocate slow ramp-down tests (10-60m real-time) to see hysteresis scale with duration.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add a dashboard panel that overlays kv-cache hit-rate, p99, and active pods during any incident window (Grafana link above).
- Create RFC for a 'falling-edge' autoscaler hook (owner: @Samir).
- File a bug on runtime allocator behavior (possible OOM/fragmentation symptom) with reproducible small-batch sequence.

Quick takeaway (for Slack/CS):
- If customers report high p99 after a traffic drop, recommend: 1) increase kv-cache TTL (short term), 2) conservative scale-down (medium), 3) we'll prototype batch-timeout smoothing (medium/long).

Raw logs & artifacts: see linked Grafana board, JIRA-1427 (investigation), and runtime PR #998 (experimental batch-timeout smoothing).

End of scratchpad.
